rv.q: A minor flaw in a splendid piece of theatre.
The last breathless line of the play is “Run!”.
Pickett’s play is a tour de force, and 1536 one of those theatrical moments that stays with you for a very long time.
Tense and original, with a creeping dread, it comes across as a first-rate thriller and a top comedy too.
It's a play that could end a couple of scenes before it does... Instead, there's a dramatic unravelling that forfeits the subtlety of its message. But it's masterly – and haunting.
By halfway through Lyndsey Turner's slow-boil production, I was wowed by the performances, taken with all the talk, still waiting for the storytelling to go beyond a canter.
Pickett is a star ascending, and her writing is about to be everywhere on stage and screen: now’s your chance to see where she started.
One of the great joys of theatre is that sometimes you’re in the room when an extraordinary voice breaks through, when something really quite special happens.
It’s a bold, essential piece of theatre that the West End should always look to have on its stages.
This is a play that we have been crying out for - and a true testament to what theatre can do.
Frankly you'd be mad to miss it.
The result is one of the sharpest, funniest and most unsettling pieces of new writing currently on the London stage.
Exceptionally well-acted and taut, 1536 is a thought-provoking and emotionally engrossing experience.

Directed by Lindsey Turner, the production is exceptionally handsome and the staging exemplary. All the action takes place on the edge of a field of corn, with a withered tree to one side (design by Max Jones), where shifts in mood are emphasised through impeccable lighting (by Jack Knowles) that moves from a warm sunny orange and a dismal grey...
I hope she’ll spare a moment for the theatre; it needs her urgent and enlightened voice.
1536 surely heralds a notable theatrical voice across several decades of this century if (at the age of 32 she is also a successful screenwriter) this continues to be Pickett’s chosen form.
This compelling production injects life into the story with deft direction, passionate performances and the skills of a fine team of creatives working behind the scenes.
This is theatre at its very best.

cn.t: Ava Pickett's debut play earns rave reviews for its sharp, modern exploration of misogyny through three Essex women reacting to Anne Boleyn's fall. Critics praise its brutal humor, electrifying performances, and devastatingly relevant feminist lens.

vr.q: This was extraordinary on arrival, and I cannot wait to tell you all about it and then demand that you all go see it.
1536 is tender and tragic, delightful and devastating, controlled and convincing. I give it five stars.
